IntroductionSlide 1 / 158
Section 1

Introduction

An automated driving system (ADS) is built in one of two ways: a modular stack of parts that people design and test one at a time, like your GP1 to GP4 stack, or one end-to-end network trained from data. Companies use one, the other, or a hybrid of both. This lecture shows how an end-to-end driver learns, why it fails, and how to compare the two designs.

IntroductionSlide 2 / 158

Who builds which design

An ADS is built as a modular stack, as one end-to-end network, or as a hybrid of the two. Companies have chosen differently.

Modular stack. People design each part and test it on its own: perception, localization, planning, control. Your GP1 to GP4 stack is one.
Hybrid. Large learned models inside a structure that people designed. Waymo builds its driver this way, with a few specialized models instead of one network [45].
End-to-end. One network from sensors to driving. Tesla says it uses “end-to-end neural networks” [34]. Wayve, led by Alex Kendall, sells end-to-end driving [47].
This lecture builds the end-to-end side, then compares it with the stack you know.
IntroductionSlide 3 / 158
Section 1 · Part 1

The Modular and the End-to-End Driver

A modular driver splits driving into parts that people design and test one at a time: perception, localization, planning, control. An end-to-end driver gives the whole job to one neural network trained from data, from the sensors to a trajectory or to commands. The difference is who decides what passes between the steps: people, or the training.

IntroductionThe Modular and the End-to-End DriverSlide 4 / 158
End-to-end learning“End-to-end learning refers to training a possibly complex learning system by applying gradient-based learning to the system as a whole” [8]

Four fields that use it. In each, one neural network goes from the raw input to the final output and skips a step that people used to design.

Speech2014 [4]
audio to text, “without requiring an intermediate phonetic representation”
Translation2014 [5]
an English sentence to a French one: “a general end-to-end approach to sequence learning”
Robot arms2016 [7]
camera images to motor torques, such as “screwing a cap onto a bottle”
Driving2016 [6]
camera pixels to steering commands (NVIDIA), today’s topic

    Section 1 · Part 2

    What End-to-End Gains

    An end-to-end driver is trained as a whole, from the sensors to the output. A 2024 survey lists what that gains over a modular stack; each gain has a price, which the lecture weighs once the clone has shown it.

    IntroductionWhat End-to-End GainsSlide 11 / 158

    Gain 1: one goal for all parts

    One goal for every part: in a modular stack, each part is trained for its own goal: the detector is scored on mAP, and the planner aims for safe, comfortable driving. End-to-end, every part, including the features it passes on, is trained for one goal: driving well. NVIDIA saw it: trained on steering alone, its network found road features, though “We never explicitly trained it to detect, for example, the outline of roads” [6].
    IntroductionWhat End-to-End GainsSlide 12 / 158

    Gain 2: no information lost

    No loss between parts: in a modular stack, each part passes on only the few things it chose, so a mistake early on carries through every later part. An object the detector misses never reaches the planner. Inside a neural network, the next layer gets the learned features, not only a chosen list.
    IntroductionWhat End-to-End GainsSlide 13 / 158

    Gain 3: less computing

    Less computing: in a modular stack, each task has its own feature extractor, so the work of finding features is done several times. End-to-end, one shared extractor finds the features once and every task uses them, so the car computes less.
    IntroductionWhat End-to-End GainsSlide 14 / 158

    Gain 4: better with more data

    Better with more data: the whole system learns from driving data, so training it on more data may make it better. This is a possibility, not a measured result. Even Alex Kendall, CEO of Wayve, gives its limit: with unlimited data, “this is really just a lookup data table”, and “that’s not economically or technically feasible” [47].
    IntroductionSlide 15 / 158

    Ways to Learn a Driver

    A network that drives has to be trained. It can copy an expert’s driving, or learn by trial from a reward, and the field sorts its methods into these two branches.

    IntroductionWays to Learn a DriverSlide 16 / 158

    Two ways to learn a driver

    A driver can copy an expert, or learn from a reward. Chen et al. sort more than 270 papers into imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) [15].

    An end-to-end driver: one network trained from data
    Imitation learning: learn from an expert's demonstrations
    Behavior cloning “reduces the problem to supervised learning” [15]Section 2 →
    Inverse optimal control uses “expert demonstrations to learn a reward function” [15]Section 2, Part 7 →
    Reinforcement learning: learn from a reward, by trial, with no expert to copy
    An RL driver on a real carSection 3 →

    The Running Example

    Ideas about learning to drive are easiest to test on a small case where everything is known: one lap of Town01, an expert that keeps the AV in its lane, and a clone that learns from the expert’s recording.

    IntroductionThe Running ExampleSlide 18 / 158

    One lap, one expert, one clone

    Today's running example: one lap of CARLA's Town01, driven by an expert and by a clone.

    1. The road: one lap of CARLA's Town01, read from its map (GP4 drives Town01 too).
    2. The expert: keeps the AV in its lane. It sees where the AV really is.
    3. The clone: learns from a recording of the expert, then drives alone. It sees what a noisy lane detector reports.
    4. We measure: how often each one finishes the lap on 20 test laps, and why the clone does not.

    Terms used in this lecture

    Eight terms the lecture uses, each with its meaning.

    TermMeaning
    PolicyA rule from what the car senses (its observation) to what it does (its action).
    ExpertThe driver whose actions are copied: a person, or a program that reads the true state from the simulator (the ground truth).
    CloneThe learned policy, trained to copy the expert.
    StateWhere the car is and how it moves: on our lap, its place on the lap (which sets the curve ahead), its offset from the lane center, its heading error.
    Open loopScoring on recorded inputs: the policy's output never moves the car.
    Closed loopScoring by driving: the policy's output moves the car, and the new state is its next input.
    WaypointsA few future positions of the car, which a controller then follows.
    Privileged informationWhat only the simulator knows, such as the true state of every car and lane.

    Section 2

    Imitation Learning

    The last section gave two ways to build a driver, the map of the field and today’s lap, expert and clone. This section takes the map’s first branch, imitation learning: learning to drive from an expert’s demonstrations. It trains the clone by behavior cloning, copying the expert’s actions, then scores it, shows why it fails and how to fix it, and ends with two other ways to learn from the same demonstrations.

    Imitation LearningSlide 22 / 158
    Section 2 · Part 1

    The Expert and Its Recording

    Behavior cloning learns a driving policy from an expert’s recorded examples. Who the expert is, and what each recorded example holds, decide what the clone can learn.

    Imitation LearningThe Expert and Its RecordingSlide 23 / 158
    Behavior cloningLearning a driving policy from an expert's recorded examples by supervised learning: each example pairs what the expert saw with what the expert did, and the policy is trained to give the expert's action for the expert's input. A policy is a rule from what the AV sees to what it does.
    1988, ALVINN
    A neural network that “takes images from a camera and a laser range finder as input and produces as output the direction the vehicle should travel”. It was trained on simulated road images [1].
    2016, NVIDIA
    “We trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) to map raw pixels from a single front-facing camera directly to steering commands”, from about 72 hours of driving [6].
    Imitation LearningThe Expert and Its RecordingSlide 24 / 158

    Who the expert is

    In our example the expert is a program. On real roads, as in NVIDIA’s 2016 work, it is a human driver. The table compares the two.

    Our exampleNVIDIA, 2016 [6]
    Who drivesa program: steer for the curve, then back to the centerhuman drivers, told to “drive as they usually do”
    What it readsthe true offset and heading (simulator only)the road, through the windshield
    Which carthe same simulated AV“a 2016 Lincoln MKZ” or “a 2013 Ford Focus with cameras placed in similar positions”
    How its action is keptstored at every stepsteering from the CAN bus, “captured simultaneously” with time-stamped video
    The expert need not drive the AV itself. Another car works when its sensors see the same view. NVIDIA stores the steering as 1/r, where r is the turning radius, “to make our system independent of the car geometry”.
    try it
    Imitation LearningThe Expert and Its RecordingSlide 25 / 158

    Recording a human expert

    NVIDIA recorded its human drivers on a real car: three cameras and the steering all feed one recorder, so the video and the steering are captured together [6].

    NVIDIA's expert is a human driver, so the recording pairs the camera video with the driver's steering [6]. Our lap's expert is a program, and its recording is a table.
    Imitation LearningThe Expert and Its RecordingSlide 26 / 158

    What the recording holds

    The recording holds one row every 0.05 s. These are three rows of run 6’s recording; the full lap has . Offset: plus is to the left.

    Time (s)Along the lap (m)Offset seen (m)Heading seen (°)Curvature ahead (1/m)Expert’s steering (°)
    • Input: the three numbers the detector and the map give. Label: the expert’s steering. Time and distance only say where the row is.
    • In the hands-on code, each column is one numpy array; nothing is written to a file.
    • NVIDIA’s rows: “single images sampled from the video, paired with the corresponding steering command (1/r)”, sampled at 10 frames per second. Views from a left and a right camera, with labels changed to “steer the vehicle back”, show the neural network off-center states [6].
    Imitation LearningThe Expert and Its RecordingSlide 27 / 158

    Behavior cloning in four steps

    Behavior cloning turns an expert’s driving into a policy in four steps: record the expert, pair each observation with the expert’s action, fit a policy to the pairs, and let the clone drive.

    1. Record the expert. Every 0.05 s, it stores the observation and the expert’s steering. Snapshot at 200 m: offset −0.27 m, heading +0.5°, curvature 0; steering −0.15°.
    2. Form the pairs. Each sample becomes one row of the array X (offset, heading, curvature ahead, 1) and one entry of y (the expert’s steering).
    3. Fit a policy. The clone steers by\[\begin{aligned}\textsf{steering} = {} & w_1 \cdot \textsf{offset} + w_2 \cdot \textsf{heading} \\ & + w_3 \cdot \textsf{curvature} + w_4 \cdot \mathsf{1}\end{aligned}\]Least squares picks the weights closest to the expert’s steering; \(w_4\) (the 1s column) is a fixed offset.
    4. Deploy the clone. It steers with no expert, so its own steering decides what it observes next.
    try it

    The expert’s steering rule

    The expert steers for the curve, then back to the lane center. Its rule has three terms, and the sliders change the curve, the offset and the heading error.

    Offset: how far the AV’s center is from the lane center, left positive. Heading error: the AV’s angle to the lane. The expert’s rule (all three numbers chosen):

    1. steer for the curve 2.4 m ahead (0.3 s at 8 m/s), as the road’s curvature asks;
    2. steer back ° for every meter of offset;
    3. steer back ° for every degree of heading error.

    Training the Clone

    Training the clone

    The clone is trained by least squares on one recorded lap: four weights fitted to all the pairs.

    1. Record: the expert drives one lap: , so pairs.
    2. Each pair: the three numbers the detector reported, and the steering the expert gave.
    3. Fit: the policy is steering = \(w_1\)·offset + \(w_2\)·heading + \(w_3\)·curvature + \(w_4\). Choose the four weights so its steering is closest to the expert's over all pairs (least squares).
    Pairoffset seen (m)heading seen (°)curvature (1/m)steering (°)

    Supervised learning with a squared loss, like a detector's box regression, but the solution has a closed form: no gradient descent. More detail: the least-squares solution

    Section 2 · Part 5

    Why the Clone Fails

    Scoring the clone gave a driver that copies the expert within 0.37° and finishes only 5 of 20 laps. A clone that scores well on recorded data can fail on the road in three ways: its small errors compound, it learns the wrong cause, or it averages two right answers.

    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsSlide 52 / 158
    Section 2 · Part 5.1

    Where the Error Grows

    The clone’s steering error is not the same everywhere: it depends on how far the AV is from the lane center. Where the expert never drove, the recording has nothing to teach.

    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsWhere the Error GrowsSlide 53 / 158

    The clone's error grows with the offset

    try it

    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsWhere the Error GrowsSlide 54 / 158

    How a small error compounds, drawn

    Four starting offsets show the same result. If the AV holds the expert’s steering for 18 m, it comes back more than if it holds the clone’s, which steers back less.

    try it
    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsWhere the Error GrowsSlide 55 / 158

    A small error, step by step

    A small error grows in four steps, because each step starts where the last one left the AV.

    1. Near the center the clone is off by 0.44°: it steers back too little, so a gust or a turn sends it farther out than the expert.
    2. Farther out, the expert would steer back 3.44° per meter, the clone only 0.38°: the error grows to 1.09° (0.25 to 0.50 m).
    3. Farther out still, it grows again: 1.78°, then 2.41°.
    4. Each step starts where the last one left the AV, so the errors add up instead of averaging out. A wheel leaves the lane.

    try it
    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsWhere the Error GrowsSlide 56 / 158
    Compounding errorThe policy's own mistakes take it to states its training data did not cover, where it makes larger mistakes.
    • In open loop this cannot happen: the next input is the recorded one, whatever the policy said.
    • Closed loop, each step starts from where the last one left the AV, so the errors add up.
    • The errors on the last slide came from the clone's own 20 test laps, not from the expert's recording.
    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsWhere the Error GrowsSlide 57 / 158

    Section 2 · Part 5.2

    Why the Weight Is Small

    The clone’s weight on the offset is 9 times too weak. The cause is the detector’s noise, and more data does not remove it.

    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsWhy the Weight Is SmallSlide 60 / 158

    How big the noise is next to the lane

    The detector’s noise is wider than the spread of the real offset, so most of what the detector reports is noise. The slider sets the noise.

    The deck's clone has σ = 0.35 (chosen for this example). Each noise level is its own training run.

    Why the offset weight is small

    The noise hides the offset, so the fit gives the offset a small weight.

    1expert, 3.44° per m2clone's fit3recorded pairs

    1. The expert stays near the center: its true offset varies by 0.15 m.
    2. The detector adds noise: 0.35 m is 2.3 times that.
    3. So most of the spread in "offset seen" is noise, and the expert's steering does not follow noise.

    What the three rows show

    The three rows compare five times the data with a detector three times quieter.

    • Five times the data moves the weight from 0.38 to 0.42, and the laps from 5 to 6.
    • Ten training runs show that a new recording alone moves the count by several laps: . So 5 to 6 is not a change we can read.
    • A detector three times quieter (0.35 / 3 = 0.117) lets the fit see the offset: the weight is and laps finish.
    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsWhy the Weight Is SmallSlide 64 / 158

    The general result

    Mistakes can grow with the square of the time. Ross and Bagnell bound behavior cloning's cost [2]: if the policy makes mistakes at rate ε on the states the expert visits (the open-loop error rate), its cost over a drive of T steps can grow up to T2ε, not Tε.

    1T² ε, the bound2T ε, no compounding

    Both axes are logarithmic: left gridlines are 100 times apart, bottom ones 10 times.

    • One mistake can take the policy off the expert's states, and from there it may keep making mistakes for the rest of the drive.
    horizon T (steps)εtry it

    More detail: the theorem, as the paper states it

    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsWhy the Weight Is SmallSlide 65 / 158

    The bound is a worst case

    The bound says what can happen, not a curve our lap must follow. Our lap shows the mechanism: a ° open-loop error, and of 20 test laps lost.

    • The bound says what can happen when one mistake sends the policy to states it never saw.
    • Our lap measures the same mechanism: 0.37° on the expert's states, and 15 of 20 test laps lost once the clone drives.
    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsSlide 66 / 158
    Section 2 · Part 5.3

    Causal Confusion

    Our clone failed through what it could see: the detector’s noise hid the offset. A clone can also fail through what it chooses to look at, a cue that comes with the right action in the recording without causing it.

    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsCausal ConfusionSlide 67 / 158

    Causal confusion

    Causal confusion makes the clone brake for the brake light. De Haan et al. trained two clones with the same network on the same driving, with one difference in the image [37].

    Clone A sees the windshield and the dashboard.
    • Training loss: low.
    • On the road: it does not drive well.
    Clone B sees the same image with the dashboard masked out.
    • Training loss: low.
    • On the road: it drives well.
    • The reason: “the dashboard has an indicator light that comes on immediately when the brake is applied, and model A wrongly learns to apply the brake only when the brake light is on” [37].
    • “Even though the brake light is the effect of braking, model A could achieve low training error by misidentifying it as the cause instead” [37].
    More inputs can make a clone worse: “access to more information can yield worse performance” [37].
    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsCausal ConfusionSlide 68 / 158

    The inertia problem

    A stopped car learns to stay stopped. Codevilla et al. trained behavior cloning in CARLA and found a failure that comes from the recording itself [38].

    1. In the recording, a stopped car nearly always stays stopped: “When the ego vehicle is stopped (e.g., at a red traffic light), the probability it stays static is indeed overwhelming in the training data” [38].
    2. The clone learns “a spurious correlation between low speed and no acceleration” [38].
    3. On the road, this gives “excessive stopping and difficult restarting” [38].

    The authors trace it to the same cause: “the inertia problem stemming from causal confusion” [38].

    In both cases the clone fits its recording, and the failure shows only when it drives.
    Imitation LearningWhy the Clone FailsSlide 69 / 158
    Section 2 · Part 5.4

    Averaging

    At junction J the route can go left or straight, and the camera image is the same for both. From a recording that holds both answers for one image, the clone learns their average, which is neither.

    Section 2 · Part 6

    Fixing the Clone

    The last part gave three causes: the clone drives where the recording never was, learns the wrong cause, and averages two right answers. Each fix targets one cause: data from the states where the clone drifts, or an input that tells two answers apart. Causal confusion has no fix that works on real driving yet.

    Imitation LearningFixing the CloneSlide 72 / 158
    Section 2 · Part 6.1

    DAgger

    DAgger lets the clone drive and asks the expert what it would steer in each state the clone reaches. The training data then covers the states the clone really visits.

    DAgger

    DAgger lets the clone drive and asks the expert to label each state, in four steps.

    try it

    • DAgger means "dataset aggregation" (Ross, Gordon and Bagnell, 2011) [3]. The paper's algorithm: "Aggregate datasets: \(D \leftarrow D \cup D_i\)"; "Train classifier \(\hat\pi_{i+1}\) on \(D\)".
    • \(D\) is all the labeled pairs so far, and \(D_i\) the pairs from iteration \(i\).
    Imitation LearningFixing the CloneDAggerSlide 75 / 158

    Who drives, who labels

    The clone steers the AV, and the expert's label for each state goes into the data.

    distance (m)try it

    The AV executes the clone's steering: .
    The data stores the expert's label for that state: .

    In iteration \(i\) the paper drives with a mix, \(\pi_i = \beta_i \pi^* + (1 - \beta_i)\hat\pi_i\) [3]. Our choice: \(\beta_1 = 1\), then \(\beta_i = 0\), so the clone drives alone, and the data keeps the expert's steering, whoever drove.

    What DAgger costs

    DAgger fixes the drift, but it has three costs. They appear one at a time.

    #Cost
    1An expert who can label any state. A program that reads the simulator's state can. A human must say what they would steer in a state they did not drive, often from a recording, after the fact.
    2A place for a bad clone to drive. The first DAgger lap is driven by the behavior-cloned clone, which left its lane on of 20 test laps. Such laps belong in a simulator, or with a safety driver.
    3A guarantee with conditions. The paper's bound is linear in \(T\), where behavior cloning's was quadratic, under conditions on the expert's ability to recover and on the class of policies.

    Red squares are laps where the clone left its lane, green ones laps it finished.

    More detail: DAgger's guarantee and its conditions

    DAgger's idea at fleet scale

    A company with a fleet uses the same idea as DAgger: find where the learned driver does poorly, and train more there.

    DAgger, on our lap. The clone drives; the expert labels every state the clone reaches; those states join the training data.
    Wayve, on a fleet. Alex Kendall, its CEO: they use unsupervised learning “to be able to cluster and find unusual or anomaly […] experiences”, then “find the scenarios that our system is […] performing poorly at and then drive the learning curriculum on those” [47].
    Both put the training data where the learned driver fails.

    Section 2 · Part 6.2

    Recovery Data

    DAgger adds the states the clone reaches, but it needs an expert who can label any state. Recovery data adds off-center states to the recording itself, each labeled with the way back.

    Imitation LearningFixing the CloneRecovery DataSlide 84 / 158

    Recovery data

    Recovery data shows the clone off-center views, each labeled with the way back to the lane. “The network must learn how to recover from mistakes” [6], but a careful driver rarely leaves the lane and real mistakes are unsafe on a public road, so the views are made.

    WhoHow the off-center states are madeThe label
    NVIDIA, 2016 [6]Two side cameras give two off-center views; the other shifts and all rotations are made from the nearest camera's image.The steering “back to the desired location and orientation in two seconds”.
    ChauffeurNet, 2018 [39]The expert's path is jittered: its midpoint up to 0.5 m in each axis, its heading up to π/3 rad (60°).A smooth path through the moved point; moves that collide or leave the road are kept, so the model “can then experience and avoid such behaviors”.
    Like DAgger, both add states the expert never drove. Unlike DAgger, no expert labels them: the label comes from geometry.
    Imitation LearningFixing the CloneRecovery DataSlide 85 / 158

    Training on off-center views

    NVIDIA's loop trains on off-center views, each labeled with the way back [6].

    Real side views and made shifts give the network off-center states; each one is labeled with the steering that leads back to the lane [6].
    Imitation LearningFixing the CloneSlide 86 / 158

    A Privileged Teacher

    Our expert already reads privileged information: the true offset, which only the simulator knows. A teacher that sees the true state can train a student that sees only the cameras.

    Imitation LearningFixing the CloneA Privileged TeacherSlide 87 / 158

    A privileged teacher

    A driver that cheats by seeing the true state trains a student that sees only the cameras. Training happens in two stages.

    The teacherThe student
    Learning by Cheating, 2019 [40]It “cheats by observing the ground-truth layout of the environment and the positions of all traffic participants”.The teacher “trains a purely vision-based sensorimotor agent”. Result: “100% success rate on all tasks in the original CARLA benchmark”.
    Roach, 2021 [41]“a reinforcement learning expert that maps bird's-eye view images to continuous low-level actions”.“a baseline end-to-end agent with monocular camera-input achieves expert-level performance”.
    Our lap has the same split: the expert reads the true offset, the clone a noisy lane detector.

    Section 2 · Part 7

    Beyond Behavior Cloning

    Behavior cloning copies the expert’s actions. The same demonstrations can teach other things: a cost that makes the expert’s path the cheapest (inverse optimal control, on the map), or a model of the world learned with the policy.

    Imitation LearningBeyond Behavior CloningSlide 93 / 158

    Cost learning

    Cost learning learns a cost from the expert, then drives the cheapest trajectory. The survey's definition: “end-to-end approaches learn a reasonable cost c(·) and use algorithmic trajectory samplers to select the trajectory τ* with the minimum cost” [15].

    1. Learn the cost: a loss that makes “the expert demonstration to have a minimal cost while others have high costs” [15].
    2. Sample candidate trajectories with an algorithm, not with the network.
    3. Drive the one with the lowest learned cost.

    Example: the Neural Motion Planner outputs “a cost volume defining the goodness of each position that the self-driving car can take within the planning horizon”, then it samples trajectories “and choose[s] the one with the minimum learned cost” [43].

    Imitation LearningBeyond Behavior CloningSlide 94 / 158

    A model of the world

    MILE learns a model of the world together with the driving policy. It is still imitation learning, with a second thing learned beside the policy.

    • MILE is “a Model-based Imitation LEarning approach to jointly learn a model of the world and a policy for autonomous driving” [44].
    • Result: “MILE improves upon prior state-of-the-art by 31% in driving score on the CARLA simulator when deployed in a completely new town and new weather conditions” [44]. The score is measured while the car drives: closed loop.
    Two ways to learn from demonstrations beyond copying the actions: learn a cost, or learn a model of the world with the policy.
    3Reinforcement Learning2 slides
    Reinforcement LearningSlide 95 / 158
    Section 3

    Reinforcement Learning

    Imitation learning needs an expert to copy. The map’s second branch, reinforcement learning, drops the expert: the driver learns from a reward, by trial. This section sets the clone and the lap aside and shows the first car that learned to drive this way.

    Reinforcement LearningSlide 96 / 158

    Reinforcement learning

    Reinforcement learning (RL): the driver learns from a reward, by trial, with no expert's actions to copy. A real car learned to follow its lane in under 30 minutes.

    • “We demonstrate the first application of deep reinforcement learning to autonomous driving” [42].
    • “From randomly initialised parameters, our model is able to learn a policy for lane following in a handful of training episodes using a single monocular image as input” [42].
    • On a 250 m road, one version drove the route “after only 11 training episodes”; the task took “under thirty minutes of training”, “all done on on-board computers” [42].
    RL needs no expert. It needs a reward and room to try and fail. Roach, the teacher of the last section, was trained this way.

    Inside the Networks

    The last two sections gave ways to train a driver; this one opens the networks they train. It sets aside the four-weight clone and the lap. It covers two published end-to-end drivers, TransFuser and UniAD, then the models that also read and write text. You see which parts of your stack such a network replaces, and which it keeps.

    Section 4 · Part 1

    Fusion and the Stack in One Network

    An end-to-end network can keep the stack’s ideas inside it. TransFuser fuses a camera and a LiDAR, and UniAD puts the stack’s tasks inside one network.

    Inside the NetworksFusion and the Stack in One NetworkSlide 99 / 158

    TransFuser

    TransFuser fuses a camera image and a LiDAR grid with attention, then predicts waypoints.

    1. Its aim: [10] “to integrate image and LiDAR representations using attention”.
    2. conv: convolution layers. attn: attention, the building block of transformers. The two branches exchange features at four resolutions.
    3. The predictor works in “an auto-regressive waypoint prediction framework” [10].
    4. “We use two PID controllers for lateral and longitudinal control” [10]: the last step is not learned.
    5. Tested closed loop in CARLA, on the CARLA Leaderboard, which has since closed [12].
    try it

    UniAD

    UniAD puts the stack's modules inside one neural network, trained together toward planning. Press a module's button to read what it does.

    • UniAD “incorporates full-stack driving tasks in one network”. “Tasks are communicated with unified query interfaces to facilitate each other toward planning” [13].
    • A query is a learned vector that collects what one module needs from the bird's-eye features. It replaces the hand-designed message between two parts.
    • Best Paper at CVPR 2023 [26]. Its planning is scored open loop, on recorded nuScenes drives [14] (the Evaluation section comes back to this).

    Section 4 · Part 2

    Vision-Language-Action Models

    The last part gave end-to-end networks that output waypoints. Vision-language-action (VLA) models add language, in and out: they also read and write text. They are the newest driving models, and they add time to every decision.

    Inside the NetworksVision-Language-Action ModelsSlide 106 / 158
    Vision-language-action model (VLA)A vision-language model (one that reads images and text and writes text) trained to output actions too: “we express the actions as text tokens and incorporate them directly into the training set of the model in the same way as natural language tokens. We refer to such category of models as vision-language-action models (VLA)” [11].
    • The term comes from RT-2, a robot manipulation model (2023).
    • For driving, the action is a trajectory, written as numbers in text, and the model can also write why.
    • Koopman warns that such reasons may not be the real cause: “a lot of the explanations are just sort of telling a story” [46].
    try itExample chosen: waypoints 1 s apart at 8 m/s, on a straight lane.

    Scoring a Driver

    The last section gave the newest models; Scoring the Clone showed open loop and closed loop on our lap. This section applies that lesson to published results. It covers why open loop misleads, the benchmarks and NVIDIA’s simulator that score in closed loop, and how GP4 scores your own stack.

    Scoring a DriverSlide 111 / 158
    Section 5 · Part 1

    Benchmarks and NVIDIA's Simulator

    A better open-loop score can lose in closed loop, on our lap and on a published benchmark. Only a closed-loop score, where the driver’s actions move the car, can judge a driver.

    Scoring a DriverBenchmarks and NVIDIA's SimulatorSlide 112 / 158

    Drive our lap

    Drive our lap yourself, in closed loop.

    Scoring a DriverBenchmarks and NVIDIA's SimulatorSlide 114 / 158

    Closed loop on recorded video

    NVIDIA tested its network in closed loop before the road, with no simulated world: it shifts each recorded frame to the new pose [6].

    NVIDIA's closed loop needs no simulated world: it moves the recorded video to where the network's steering would have put the car [6]. On our lap, the simulator plays this role.

      Scoring a DriverSlide 119 / 158
      Section 5 · Part 2

      GP4

      The benchmarks score published drivers in closed loop. GP4 does the same for your own stack: its script scores a drive.

      Scoring a DriverGP4Slide 120 / 158

      GP4 scores your stack in closed loop

      GP4 runs your stack: your commands decide where the AV goes next. You run your route twice, with your EKF pose and with the true pose, among 40 vehicles and 80 walkers.

      tools/evaluate_run.py scores each drive until the AV first comes within 2 m of the goal, and reports:

      • route completion: 1 at arrival, else 1 minus the road distance left over the route’s length;
      • collisions and pedestrian hits;
      • red-light violations: crossing a stop line on red faster than 1 m/s;
      • cross-track error and mean speed.
      Grading, on a held-out route: points for route completion at least 0.8 of the reference solution's, and for no more red-light violations or pedestrian hits than it.
      Scoring a DriverGP4Slide 121 / 158

      What GP4's script measures on a drive

      GP4’s script measures five things on each drive. Click a tag to see where each one comes from.

      From tools/evaluate_run.py: 1 the road distance left to the goal (a 2 m circle) over the route's length; 2 a collision; 3 a person inside the box 2.5 m ahead and behind and 1.1 m to each side, with the AV above 0.5 m/s; 4 the stop line crossed on red above 1 m/s; 5 the distance to the planned path.       Section 6

      Modular or End-to-End?

      Scoring a Driver gave closed-loop scores and showed why open-loop ones mislead. This section uses them to compare the two designs: first what end-to-end costs, then the two designs side by side and how to compare them fairly, then GP5. Your final report evaluates your modular pipeline, and end-to-end driving is the optional GP5.

      Modular or End-to-End?Slide 124 / 158
      Section 6 · Part 1

      What End-to-End Costs

      The four gains of the first section come with costs, and the same survey lists four. The last is the problem the clone showed on our lap: it drives into states the expert never showed.

      Modular or End-to-End?What End-to-End CostsSlide 125 / 158

      Cost 1: hard to open, a black box

      Hard to open: in your stack, you read each topic and find the part that failed. An end-to-end network has no topics inside to read, so people call it a black box. Alex Kendall, CEO of Wayve, replies that it is “naive” to expect a complex intelligent machine to be “strictly interpretable to the point where you can point to a single line of code” [47].
      Modular or End-to-End?What End-to-End CostsSlide 126 / 158

      Cost 2: no proof of safety

      No safety proof: an end-to-end network learns how to drive from data, so no math proves that it always drives safely. Tests cover only the states someone tried.
      Modular or End-to-End?What End-to-End CostsSlide 127 / 158

      Why testing cannot prove safety

      Phil Koopman, who studies the safety of self-driving cars, gives two reasons why testing alone cannot show that a learned driver is safe [46].

      Covering every neuron. A chip test can exercise every gate and show that it is there. A network is different: “if you exercise all the neurons in an artificial neural network, it doesn’t prove anything” [46].
      Driving more miles. Brute-force testing takes about a billion miles, “and you’ve probably retrained the machine learning 100 times in that billion miles. So none of it counts” [46].
      The design and the result come apart: “Did the machine learning learn what I wanted to? I don’t know. Let’s drive it around and find out” [46].
      Modular or End-to-End?What End-to-End CostsSlide 128 / 158

      Two views on proving safety

      The skeptic and the advocate agree on the problem: training data alone does not make a learned driver safe.

      Phil Koopman, who studies the safety of self-driving cars: testing a learned driver proves little, since over a billion test miles “none of it counts” [46].
      Alex Kendall, CEO of Wayve, which sells end-to-end driving: “we can’t just pump more data in” and “hope that hallucinations go away”. The design must be “functionally safe”, with “a […] robust […] behavioral safety case” [47].
      Both say a learned driver needs a safety argument beyond its data. Kendall calls building one a matter of “architectural challenges” [47].
      Modular or End-to-End?What End-to-End CostsSlide 129 / 158

      Cost 3: rare cases, the long tail

      Rare cases: a long tail means many rare situations, each with few examples in the driving data. A network that learns only from data learns those cases poorly, and for end-to-end driving this problem is especially serious.
      Modular or End-to-End?What End-to-End CostsSlide 130 / 158

      A heavy tail, not only a long one

      Koopman separates two problems: a long tail is rare events, and a heavy tail is a great many different rare events [46].

      “Long tail is rare events, but a heavy tail means there’s a lot of things. So maybe this is once per billion miles, but if you have a billion of them, you’re going to see one every mile. And if you fix it, that doesn’t help you” [46].

      His example, worked out (our arithmetic, if sightings come independently, as a Poisson count): an event that happens once per billion miles, and 100 million miles of driving data.

      1. Expected sightings: 100,000,000 / 1,000,000,000 = 0.1.
      2. Chance of never seeing it: e−0.1 = 0.90.

      So the data most likely holds no example of it at all; in his words, “you’ve never seen it probably” [46].

      Modular or End-to-End?What End-to-End CostsSlide 131 / 158

      Cost 4: states the expert never showed

      Different states from the expert’s: the network learns from the states the expert drove through, but when it drives, the states it reaches differ from the expert’s. Today’s running example measures what that does.
      Modular or End-to-End?Slide 132 / 158
      Section 6 · Part 2

      Comparing the Designs

      The modular stack and the end-to-end driver can be set side by side, even inside one car. A fair comparison scores both the same way.

      Modular or End-to-End?Comparing the DesignsSlide 133 / 158

      The two designs, side by side

      The two designs differ in what they are built from and what they need.

      try it
      Modular (your stack)End-to-end
      Built fromparts people design, each with its own testone neural network trained on driving data
      Between partsmessages people chose: boxes, a pose, a pathwhatever the neural network learned
      Trained foreach part's own scorethe driving output
      Debuggingread each topic, find the partlook at outputs and any readable parts inside (UniAD)
      Data it needslabels for each part, such as boxes for a detectordriving data; for DAgger, an expert that can label any state
      Both are tested the same way at the end: closed loop, on the routes and scenarios that matter.

      More detail: two companies' own claims

      Modular or End-to-End?Comparing the DesignsSlide 134 / 158

      Where the line between them blurs

      Real systems are not purely one design or the other, even in the words of an end-to-end advocate.

      • Modular stacks learn too. Alex Kendall, CEO of Wayve: “anyone who’s worth a grain of salt will use deep learning in various parts of the stack” [47].
      • Some sit in between. Waymo describes “fewer, high-capacity, specialized foundation models”, not “a single, black box” [45].
      • Mixing is not free. In Kendall’s view, hybrid approaches “can get the worst of both worlds or just add cost and complexity” [47].
      The question is less “which design” than where to draw the line between learned parts and written rules.
      Modular or End-to-End?Comparing the DesignsSlide 135 / 158

      One car, two designs

      Either design runs on this car; only the program changes. Koopman calls sensors a data choice: “lots and lots of lower quality data”, or “a much smaller amount of very high quality data” [46].

      Design:

      Modular or End-to-End?Comparing the DesignsSlide 136 / 158

      A fair comparison, in four steps

      A fair comparison of two drivers needs four steps. Step through them with the buttons.

      1. Same routes and scenarios, none used in training or tuning. Your final report does this for your modular pipeline: three scenarios the instructor provides, unseen during development.
      2. Closed loop, with the same metrics: route completion, collisions, red lights, as GP4's script reports them.
      3. Several runs, and report the spread: our clone finished 2 to 9 laps of 20 depending only on the training run.
      4. Say what each one was given: sensors, the map, the route, privileged information (a state only the simulator knows, like the expert's true offset). CARLA's Leaderboard banned “any privilege information offered by the CARLA simulator” [25].
      try it
      Modular or End-to-End?Comparing the DesignsSlide 137 / 158

      Handling a new exception

      In Koopman’s view, a new exception costs the two designs different work: a few lines of code, or a data collection job [46]. His example: blue stop signs, found in parking lots in Hawaii.

      Modular stack. “if you notice something weird, it’s not so bad writing a manual rule to handle it”: blue stop signs go into the detector’s training data, and the planner stays as it is, “because a stop sign’s a stop sign” [46].
      End-to-end. “if you discover […] an exception, you have to retrain the whole thing”: the network must learn that blue stop signs are stop signs “without it necessarily knowing what a stop sign really is” [46].
      “You haven’t changed the need to handle the exceptions, but you’ve converted it from a programming job of a few lines of code into a data collection job” [46].
      Modular or End-to-End?Slide 138 / 158
      Section 6 · Part 3

      GP5: An Optional Project

      GP5 is optional and not graded: it keeps your GP1 to GP3 nodes and GP4’s planner, and replaces GP4’s behavior and controller nodes with a learned model.

      Modular or End-to-End?GP5: An Optional ProjectSlide 139 / 158
      Section 6 · Part 3.1

      The Project

      GP5 is an optional end-to-end project on your own stack. It keeps most of your nodes and puts one learned node in place of two.

      Modular or End-to-End?GP5: An Optional ProjectThe ProjectSlide 140 / 158

      GP5, an optional project

      GP5 is optional and not graded: no points, no bonus, nothing due and nothing submitted. It does not count toward the group-project grade or the final report.

      What you do
      Keep your GP1 to GP3 nodes and GP4's planner, remove GP4's behavior and controller nodes, and add one learned model in their place. It reads the front camera image and a short text command, and outputs steering, throttle and brake.
      What you get
      No starter code and no reference solution. The GP5 page lists the files you create and the GP4 files you reuse.
      Your team
      Your GP4 team. You can show the drive and a comparison table to the instructor, by email or in office hours.
      Today's lecture gives the ideas behind GP5, and GP4's closed loop and scoring script test your model.
      Modular or End-to-End?GP5: An Optional ProjectThe ProjectSlide 141 / 158

      GP5 in the node graph

      GP5 replaces two nodes with one learned model. Click a tag.

      1 kept, your GP1 to GP3 nodes and GP4's planner_node. 2 removed, GP4's behavior_node and controller_node. 3 added, vla_node. The GP1 to GP3 nodes send tracks and the pose to the planner; vla_node reads the camera image and the speed, takes the text command from the route, and publishes the vehicle command.

      Modular or End-to-End?GP5: An Optional ProjectSlide 142 / 158
      Section 6 · Part 3.2

      GP5's Model

      The project adds one node, vla_node, in place of your behavior and controller nodes. Inside it is a model of which you train only one part.

      Modular or End-to-End?GP5: An Optional ProjectGP5's ModelSlide 143 / 158

      GP5's model in three parts

      GP5’s model has two frozen encoders, one trained decoder and six fixed commands.

      • Two frozen CLIP encoders (a pre-trained image and text model), 512 numbers each. You do not train them.
      • One input: the two vectors and the speed, 512 + 512 + 1 = 1,025 numbers.
      • A small decoder that you train, a multi-layer perceptron (a few fully connected layers), gives three numbers in the ranges of the vehicle command.
      • Six fixed commands, such as “follow the road” and “turn left at the intersection”: the text input is a choice among six constant vectors.
      Modular or End-to-End?GP5: An Optional ProjectGP5's ModelSlide 144 / 158

      GP5's model, drawn

      The drawing shows how the image, the command and the speed become one input and then a vehicle command. Click a tag to read each part.

      1 two frozen CLIP encoders, 512 numbers each. 2 with the speed, one input of 512 + 512 + 1 = 1,025 numbers. 3 the decoder is the only part you train.

      Modular or End-to-End?GP5: An Optional ProjectGP5's ModelSlide 145 / 158

      Where GP5's model sits

      GP5’s model fits into the family of end-to-end drivers from this lecture.

      So GP5's model is close to conditional imitation: a camera-driven policy with a six-way command. It is much smaller than DriveVLM or Alpamayo, and it does not write text.
      Modular or End-to-End?GP5: An Optional ProjectGP5's ModelSlide 146 / 158

      Where that leaves us

      Five points sum up the lecture. Each one links to the slide that taught it.

      • Behavior cloning is supervised learning on an expert's drive. Our clone (run 6) copied the expert within 0.37° and finished 5 test laps of 20; ten runs finish 2 to 9. slide 23
      • Its error grew from 0.44° near the center to 2.41° near the lane's edge: compounding error, in states the recording never showed. slide 53
      • DAgger adds those states, labeled by the expert: 19 of 20 laps, in 10 of 10 training runs. slide 74
      • Junctions need the route's command. End-to-end neural networks range from TransFuser to UniAD to VLAs; their authors report 0.41 s (DriveVLM) and 0.099 s (Alpamayo 1), on different chips. slide 70
      • Judge any driver in closed loop: open-loop scores favored the clone that failed. slide 112

      Overview
      Turn your phone sideways to read the slides.

      Keys

      → Space PgDnnext: on a step table, the next row first
      ← PgUpback
      ↑the whole section; a second press, the table of contents; Esc the overview of the lecture
      H ?this window, on or off (Esc closes it too)
      Ctrl Ksearch the slides by their words (a term, a number, a name); ↑ ↓ pick a slide, Enter goes, Esc closes
      a number, Entergo to that slide: type its number (shown top right as slide / total), then Enter; G opens the same field
      Click the slide numbergo to a slide: the number becomes a field; type a slide number, Enter goes, Esc cancels
      Tlight or dark theme
      Ffull screen on or off
      D Cpen on or off; clear the drawing (it also clears when the slide changes)
      Llaser pointer on or off
      + −zoom; scroll or pinch zooms too, and a drag moves the overview (no zoom in full screen)
      a sliderdrag it, or click it and use ↑ ↓; ← → always change the slide; Esc gives ↑ ↓ back to the slides

      Frames marked try it have controls. Click a box or a section to fly to it. The top right corner shows the slide controls when the mouse rests there.

      Colors

      The expert, on every plot and drawing. The behavior-cloned clone. A clone trained with DAgger. Lane edges: where a wheel leaves the lane. What moves or changes now: the value you set, the step running. Text a slider or button just changed. An issue, or a lap that left its lane. Reached: a lap that finished.

      Every number a frame shows comes from the deck's own measurements or from the hands-on model (numpy, training run 6, test laps 100 to 119). A value chosen for an example says so. The controls replay that model's runs; none of them invents a number.

      How this deck is made

      One web page with no framework: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the live figures drawn in SVG. Math: KaTeX 0.16.11. Fonts: Fira Sans and Fira Mono (SIL Open Font License), carried in the page. A Python script builds the page from one file per section. The lap, the expert, the clone and DAgger run in a numpy model that writes the data the page replays; the figures come from Python (Matplotlib), TikZ and Inkscape. Vehicle icons: Stone, the Noun Project. The 3D Tesla Model 3 is “VEHICLE - TESLA MODEL 3” by Thcyrax (Sketchfab, CC BY 4.0), drawn with three.js r128 (MIT license).
